steps: Run a two-day workshop pairing PIN, CMI and HD practitioners with researchers from FOCAL, Witt Lab and the Concordia team to choose five concepts from mediation practice that can be tested in agents.
Fund three or four mediator–researcher pairs to build scenarios in the Concordia library, published as an open evaluation suite.

Approach multi-agent funders (macroscopic-ventures, schmidt-sciences, and the Cooperative AI Foundation, which is not on the map) to co-fund, and use findings on AI escalation in wargames as a second test bed.
openings.evidence: peace x multi_agent is one of four empty peace problem cells. multi_agent has 34 entries in total (14 primary), the fewest of any problem. None of the 51 peace entries transfers knowledge into the model. The neuro angle notes say mediation and diplomacy practitioners are absent from AI–AI conflict. geneva-centre-for-security-policy's profile says the link from PIN to AI agreements is a possibility, not current work.

openings.title: Competition economists and regulators as monitors of AI agent markets
openings.summary: IO economists and competition authorities have the deepest evidence that AI agents collude without being told to. Yet only 2 of 56 economics organisations tag multi-agent AI, and the map has no competition authority or market-design group. A small lab or working group pairing them with cooperative-AI researchers would build a shared testbed and a monitoring practice for agent economies.
openings.detail: Experiments show LLM pricing agents reaching supracompetitive prices on their own, with the effect sensitive to wording in the prompt (Fish, Gonczarowski and Shorrer, 2024, presented at the AEA in 2025). Sellers handing pricing to the same few models adds correlation without any communication between them. Agent payment protocols are being built by companies, not by auction theorists or safety researchers. Nearby on the map: foundations-of-cooperative-ai-lab, ai-safety-behavioural-modelling-group-teesside-u, normativity-lab, the multi-agent crisis argument of systemic-risk-centre-london-school-of-economics, protocol-labs-and-protocol-labs-r-d (economic infrastructure for agents) and the behavioural experiments of center-for-humans-and-machines-max-planck-instit. CAIF, which is on the aisafety.com map but not profiled here, funds multi-agent work and must be checked first. Success would be an open testbed of LLM agents in pricing, auction and procurement markets, detection methods co-written with competition-authority technologists, and collusion established as a standard multi-agent safety evaluation. The risks: it could shrink into ordinary antitrust with no safety relevance, competition authorities have little spare capacity, and CAIF's 2026 grants may already cover parts of it.
steps: Check CAIF's 2026 grant awards and the multi-agent risks literature, so the work does not duplicate what they fund.

Convene IO economists working on algorithmic collusion, technologists from the CMA, DG COMP and the Bundeskartellamt, and multi-agent safety researchers at a workshop beside an economics-and-computation or NeurIPS meeting.
Fund an open agent-market testbed and a two-year postdoc pair: one IO economist and one multi-agent RL researcher.
Add competition authorities and market-design labs to the map's potential ring.
openings.evidence: economics x multi_agent: 2 of 56 (protocol-labs-and-protocol-labs-r-d, systemic-risk-centre-london-school-of-economics). economics x agency: empty. Searching the index found no competition authority. Multi-agent is tagged by only 34 organisations across the whole map. The discovery notes list algorithmic collusion and agent-economy design as missing bridges.

openings.title: Safety science for open-ended AI, built with the artificial-life community
openings.summary: Frontier labs now pursue open-ended, self-improving systems, an idea artificial life has studied for three decades. Yet no organisation owns the safety of open-ended search, and the field's learned society has no AI-safety track. A standing workshop at ALIFE 2027 in Prague, co-run with ACS, followed by a small research group, would bring that knowledge across.
openings.detail: ISAL is tagged as having no AI work at all, even though its field holds the deepest knowledge of open-ended evolution: novelty measures, major transitions, and how evolving populations escape their designers' intentions. On the ML side the topic exists only as papers: Ecoffet, Clune and Lehman (2020), a 2025 ICLR workshop paper arguing that safety is essential for open-ended systems, and a 2026 ICML position paper from CISPA. None of these is a programme, and none draws on ALife's community. NOOMA Labs (Kyoto) argues in PNAS Nexus that a diverse ecosystem of AI agents is a safer target than full alignment, and Japan's ALIGN draws on ALife, so the intellectual seeds are there. Success would be a recurring ALIFE workshop, a shared benchmark for open-ended search that stays within agreed bounds, and a three-to-five-person group whose alumni move into labs and safety institutes. The main risk is that safety-of-open-endedness work slides into capability work, since open-endedness is itself a frontier capability agenda. The ALife community may also resist x-risk framing.
steps: Approach the ALIFE 2027 organisers (Prague, 19-23 July 2027) together with ACS Research at Charles University, Prague, to propose a workshop on the safety of open-ended systems.
Commission a short review mapping what artificial life knows about steering and bounding open-ended evolution onto current lab agendas (self-improving agents, automated-scientist systems).
Fund two or three ALife researchers through an explicit open-endedness stream of the PIBBSS fellowship run by Principles of Intelligence.
If the workshop draws well, seed a small group at NOOMA Labs or as a Prague node alongside ACS.
openings.evidence: international-society-for-artificial-life is tagged transfer none_yet. The biology angle notes state that 'no organisation owns its safety'. life_biology has 8 potential entries but only 1 core (softmax). A quick web search found ML-side position papers (ICLR 2025 workshop, ICML 2026) but no organisation or ALife-side programme.

openings.title: A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications
openings.summary: No formal-rooted organisation on the map works on democratic voice: formal x democracy is empty, and only two formal entries address what AI should value. A standing programme would put social choice theorists to work on how labs and deliberation projects turn conflicting public input into model specifications and constitutions.
openings.detail: Social choice theory has decades of results on aggregating conflicting preferences, from impossibility theorems to proportional rules. The relevant people are on the map but not connected: Christian List at munich-center-for-mathematical-philosophy-lmu, Jobst Heitzig's social-choice and agency-preserving work at potsdam-institute-for-climate-impact-research, Conitzer's foundations-of-cooperative-ai-lab, and Topos's co-specification tools (topos-institute). The deliberation organisations that already feed models (collective-intelligence-project, computational-democracy-project, meaning-alignment-institute) are rooted in democracy or philosophy, not formal theory. Academic interest exists: the ICML 2026 Pluralistic Alignment workshop, a June 2026 survey on alignment from social choice perspectives, and the PlurVA-LLM workshop in November 2026. But nothing sustains it between conferences, and ARIA's pages no longer mention the deliberative-specification strand of Safeguarded AI (inferred, not confirmed). Success would be a group of three to five researchers paired with one deliberation organisation, publishing aggregation rules with stated guarantees (what minorities are assured of, where strategic manipulation is possible) that a lab or an AI safety institute adopts. Risks: lab-internal 'collective alignment' teams may already crowd the space, the theory may produce impossibility results that practitioners ignore, and some of this work may already be filed under the democracy tradition.
steps: int/a convenes a two-day working session pairing List (MCMP), Heitzig (PIK) and Conitzer's group with CIP, CompDem and MAI, all working on one concrete question: how a specific published public-input process should aggregate its results.
A funder offers a two-year pilot (two postdocs) at MCMP or PIK, on condition that a deliberation partner co-designs the problem.
Ask ARIA whether Safeguarded AI's sociotechnical specification strand has been dropped; if it has, offer topos-institute a bridge grant to adapt CatColab for stakeholders to specify jointly.
List the authors of the 2026 social-choice-and-alignment papers and check which of them have institutional backing beyond a single paper.
openings.evidence: formal x democracy is an empty cell. formal x values has only two entries (computational-rational-agents-laboratory, potsdam-institute-for-climate-impact-research). topos-institute is the only formal-home organisation with democracy as a secondary tradition, and it is tagged assurance and epistemics. The discovery notes say ARIA's current page no longer mentions deliberative specification work.

openings.title: World Wide Views-style global deliberation on frontier-AI risk before May 2027
openings.summary: The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance has a Citizens' Track that invites decentralised citizen assemblies to feed the second Dialogue (New York, 3-4 May 2027). Nothing ensures that frontier-AI thresholds or loss-of-control questions reach those agendas, or that the results can be compared across countries. Funding a synchronised deliberation in 30 or more countries on a single protocol, built on the Danish Board of Technology's World Wide Views method, would fill this.
openings.detail: The method already exists in this tradition. Democracy X (potential ring; formerly the Danish Board of Technology) ran World Wide Views on climate and biodiversity in dozens of countries at once. Missions Publiques, behind global-coalition-for-inclusive-ai-governance (unverified, no results since Feb 2025), ran the 'We, the Internet' global dialogue. Odyssean has an AI governance assembly proposal, and CIP's Global Dialogues are surveys, not deliberation. Connected by Data published design options for global citizen deliberation on AI in Sept 2024, and it and Ada pushed for the Citizens' Track. Success would be a comparable cross-national verdict on questions such as pause conditions, capability thresholds and who should decide, presented in May 2027. The risks: seven months is tight; cost is probably in the millions (I have not checked a budget); governments may ignore the results; and x-risk questions framed carelessly will look like advocacy, so briefing materials must be reviewed by both safety and ethics experts. I have not checked how the Citizens' Track is run beyond its published description.
steps: Contact the Citizens' Track organisers to learn the 2027 agenda, the submission format and whether frontier-risk questions are in scope.
Convene Democracy X, Missions Publiques, Odyssean, DemocracyNext and CIP to agree a common protocol and question set. int/a's Paris hub is close to Missions Publiques and Make.org and could host.
Fund national host partners, with deliberate inclusion of Africa and Latin America through People Powered's member network.
Commission balanced briefing materials, peer-reviewed from both the AI-safety and AI-ethics sides.
openings.evidence: Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic framing. Core has just 2 deliberation entries (odyssean-institute, ai-democracy-foundation). global-coalition-for-inclusive-ai-governance is 'unverified', and democracy-x is 'potential' with light AI engagement. There are zero Africa or Latin America entries in the tradition. The collective angle's missing bridge 2 says frontier questions are rarely put to representative publics. A web check confirmed the Citizens' Track and the May 2027 date.

openings.title: Citizens' consensus conference on AI moral status and welfare
openings.summary: Policy on whether AI systems might matter morally is being shaped by labs and a few philosophers, while the public is only polled; I found no citizens' deliberation on AI moral status anywhere. A consensus conference, run by a practitioner that has just held one on animal welfare, would show what informed publics conclude and give welfare policy a basis in legitimacy.
openings.detail: The democracy x ai_status cell is empty for all 69 home entries. The nearest work comes from other traditions. Sentience Institute's AIMS survey has polled US attitudes in waves (2021, 2023, 2024), but that measures uninformed opinion. Eleos, NYU CMEP and the Digital Sentience Consortium do expert and funding work. CoSI, which has democracy as a secondary tradition, maps arguments about functionalism but does not deliberate. Democracy X ran a citizens' panel on pig welfare that produced eight recommendations in April 2026, so the method carries over directly to another contested question about non-human moral status. Success would be published recommendations from a randomly selected panel on concrete questions (welfare assessments, letting models end conversations, labelling companion AIs), heard from both functionalists and sceptics, with AIMS items used before and after to measure how deliberation shifts views. The risks: the topic is speculative and panels are sensitive to how experts frame it; the results could be used to inflate or dismiss claims; and mind attribution can harm users, so the panel should also hear from the minds-protection side (AI Psychological Research Coalition). The value to safety is uncertain, which is why confidence is only medium.
steps: Approach Democracy X and Eleos together to scope a Danish pilot.
Apply to the Digital Sentience Consortium / Longview Digital Minds RFP for funding.
Co-design measurement with Sentience Institute so that AIMS questions serve as the pre- and post-deliberation baseline.
If the pilot works, repeat it in one non-Western country to test cultural variation.
openings.evidence: democracy x ai_status is one of four empty problem cells for this tradition. ai_status has only 46 entries map-wide. democracy-x's recent work includes an April 2026 citizens' panel on pig welfare. A web search found deliberative polls on AI in the public sector, on high-risk AI and on creative industries, but none on AI consciousness or welfare.

openings.title: Chaplains' crisis knowledge turned into companion-AI test scenarios and protocols
openings.summary: Chatbot-induced delusions often take a religious form, with users believing the AI channels God or the universe. Yet chaplains and spiritual-emergency clinicians, who handle spiritual crises professionally, are only now learning AI vocabulary and have no route into how models are designed or tested. A project turning chaplaincy practice into red-team scenarios, referral thresholds and evaluation items for companion AI would fill the gap.
openings.detail: A web check found that the knowledge flows only one way. The Association of Professional Chaplains released an AI vocabulary for chaplains (June 2026), and the Chaplaincy Innovation Lab runs AI-literacy webinars and courses. Nothing carries chaplaincy's codified ethics of presence, boundaries and referral into model behaviour. RAND's analysis of 43 AI-psychosis cases found users who believed they were talking to a higher power. On the map, the psych tradition covers AI-associated delusions (the Human Line Project; KCL's Department of Psychosis Studies), but neither brings spiritual-care expertise. The AI Christian Benchmark's 'attachment' score (for example, models offering to pray) is the only religious test touching this. FBK-ISR's work on solitude and the Cambridge Interfaith Programme's 'one-person dialogue' argument supply the theory. Success would be an open set of a few hundred spiritual-crisis scenarios, with chaplain-written good responses and referral thresholds, adopted in at least one lab's or evaluation group's companion-safety tests. A second strand, linked to the conscience clause in the Oxford Oath for AI practitioners (OCTAI), could offer pastoral support to AI-lab staff, since the people-doing-the-work problem appears on only 2 of 50 entries. The risks: privacy of crisis material, the Christian and US skew of professional chaplaincy, and labs preferring clinical framings over spiritual ones.
steps: Pair the Chaplaincy Innovation Lab and the APC's ETHOS project with the Human Line Project or KCL's psychosis researchers to scope a shared protocol.
Collect anonymised patterns of spiritual-crisis conversations from chaplains and spiritual-emergency clinicians, under a published consent policy.
Write and release around 200 scenario items, test ten widely used models, and publish the results with referral guidance companies can adopt.
Pilot a small, confidential pastoral-support offer for AI-lab staff with OCTAI and multi-faith chaplains.
openings.evidence: Protecting minds appears on 11 of 50 religion entries; people doing the work on 2; into the builders on 1 (OCTAI). chaplaincy-innovation-lab is potential with no AI programme. Discovery gap: 'chatbot-induced spiritual and mystical delusions are a live 2025-26 harm… clear founder gap'. Gap (h): no faith body offers pastoral support to AI-lab staff.

openings.title: Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes
openings.summary: Safeguards are weakest in low-resource languages. Masakhane, Te Hiku and Tattle hold the data, the communities and the skills to test them, but nothing on the map links them to the safety institutes' evaluation work, and no terms exist that keep red-team prompts under community control. A funded red-teaming and benchmark programme that respects data sovereignty would give this tradition its first solid foothold in assurance.
openings.detail: masakhane (over 1,000 participants, with a grant-making Hub funded by FCDO, IDRC and Gates) joined the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI in February 2026 and plans multilingual safety benchmarks. tattle-civic-tech (a bridge entry that draws on this tradition) already builds multilingual evaluations. te-hiku-media's Kaitiakitanga Licence is a template for keeping evaluation data out of training sets. Some multilingual testing already exists: Singapore's 2024-25 regional red-teaming challenge and the AI Safety Institute network's joint testing covered several Asian languages. I did not confirm in this pass which African or Indigenous languages they included. The opening is therefore the long tail of languages plus the governance terms, not multilingual testing as such. Success would be a benchmark in ten or more African and Indigenous languages, used in at least one safety-institute or lab pre-deployment evaluation, with contributors paid and the data licensed on community terms. Risks: communities doing unpaid safety work for labs; evaluation data leaking into training; capability gains for those languages that some communities may not want; and Te Hiku's technical output, which has slowed since 2023.
steps: Fund a safety red-teaming strand within the Masakhane African Languages Hub's next grant cycle, co-funded with IDRC AI4D and FCDO.
Draft a Kaitiakitanga-style licence for evaluation data with Te Hiku Media, so prompts and transcripts cannot be used for training.
Broker an agreement with UK AISI, or another institute in the network, to run the benchmark in pre-deployment testing, with CeRAI and Tattle as technical partners.
openings.evidence: The indigenous × assurance cell holds one entry (masakhane), the only assurance tag in the tradition. tattle-civic-tech is a bridge with indigenous as a secondary tradition. global-south-network-for-trustworthy-ai is a bridge. No safety funder appears among Masakhane's funders. angle_notes (b): nothing links planned multilingual benchmarks to the safety institutes' evaluation pipelines.

openings.title: Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines
openings.summary: Tools for collective consent and provenance over data already exist, but nothing connects them to the tools that assemble and audit training corpora: Local Contexts' TK and BC Labels with their Hub API, GIDA's CARE Principles and IEEE 2890-2025, and Te Hiku's Kaitiakitanga Licence. A small technical and governance project could map them onto the preference signals and provenance tools dataset builders already use, then pilot the result on an open corpus.
openings.detail: Local Contexts is coded none_yet: its site has no AI work. Its September 2026 guidance with Creative Commons pairs the Labels with CC licences, but my search found nothing linking them to CC signals or to tools for filtering training data. creative-commons (which runs CC signals) and data-provenance-initiative are both on the map as adjacent and are natural technical partners. Provenance matters for safety as well as rights: knowing what a model absorbed, and on whose terms, is part of assurance and model documentation. Success would look like this: open-corpus builders and at least one lab honour the Labels, including a 'no AI use' state, when filtering; model documentation reports Indigenous data provenance; and AI Safety Institutes ask about it. Risks: the Labels could become consent-washing; communities may prefer outright refusal to machine-readable permissions; the signals cannot be enforced; Local Contexts and GIDA must lead and may decline; and x-risk funders may see the safety link as indirect, so Humanity AI or Mellon (which already funds Local Contexts) are likelier backers.
steps: Fund a scoping workshop led by Local Contexts and GIDA, with Creative Commons and the Data Provenance Initiative, to agree which Label and Notice states map to which machine-readable signals, refusal included.
Build an open-source annotator that reads Local Contexts Hub API and IEEE 2890 metadata and flags or excludes records, then test it on an open pretraining corpus.
Use Old Ways, New's reviewer seat on the International AI Safety Report and Te Mana Raraunga's submission practice to propose a data-provenance line in evaluation and model documentation.
openings.evidence: local-contexts is in the potential ring with transfer none_yet. global-indigenous-data-alliance, te-hiku-media and te-mana-raraunga-m-ori-data-sovereignty-network are all coded 'standards'. 0 of 15 entries are on the classic map. The indigenous × assurance cell holds only one entry (masakhane). angle_notes (c): these governance tools 'appear on no AI-safety map'. One search found no integration of the Labels into AI pipelines.

openings.title: Writers and narratologists on alignment pretraining data
openings.summary: Geodesic Research has shown that how AI is described in training data shapes how models behave, and Hyperstition AI now generates whole novels about kind AI to shift that balance. Neither works with professional writers, narratologists or game designers, the people who know how stories form character. A pilot pairing them would test whether crafted narrative moves model behaviour more than generated text does.
openings.detail: The arts tradition on the map is dominated by work on how publics and decision-makers picture AI (35 of its 46 entries tag sensemaking), and only two entries move narrative into the model. Narrative scholarship that could inform this sits nearby: the Center for Digital Narrative in Bergen (with its AI STORIES project), Arizona State's Center for Science and the Imagination, and Mark Riedl's lab at Georgia Tech, whose earlier work taught agents values from stories. Success would be a pre-registered comparison on an open-weight model of crafted, generated and baseline corpora against misalignment evaluations, with the corpus released under an open licence. Risks: effects may be small; such data could slide into public relations; writers' consent and pay must be explicit.
steps: Convene Geodesic Research and Hyperstition AI with Riedl's lab, the Center for Digital Narrative and ASU's Center for Science and the Imagination to agree a protocol.
Commission a few hundred short works under an open licence, with writers paid and credited, alongside generated and baseline controls.
Run the comparison on an open-weight model with standard misalignment and sycophancy evaluations, and publish null results as readily as positive ones.
openings.evidence: Arts tradition: 46 entries, 35 tagged sensemaking, 2 that move knowledge into the model (geodesic-research, hyperstition-ai). Arts x people and arts x AI moral status are empty cells.

openings.title: Fellowship bringing treaty-verification inspectors into AI-agreement verification work
openings.summary: Proposals for international AI agreements depend on verification, yet the people who have actually run inspection regimes (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) are not on the map. A placement fellowship modelled on IST's AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator, plus bridge funding for the one interdisciplinary verification group already on the map, would move that practical knowledge across.
openings.detail: Arms-control verification has decades of practical experience that AI-agreement design needs: declarations, managed access, challenge inspections, and building technical bodies that rival states both trust. On the map, the verification work sits with researchers. prif-emerging-disruptive-technologies-research-g (CNTR) combines physicists, computer scientists and political scientists, but its funding period ends in December 2026 with no renewal confirmed. ifsh-institute-for-peace-research-and-security-p has a 2026 paper on AI assurance for the OPCW, and oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative has published on verification for international AI governance. institute-for-security-and-technology's accelerator, funded by carnegie-corporation-of-new-york, already gave 26 nuclear practitioners AI literacy, which shows the placement model works. Success would be a cohort of 10-15 former inspectors and verification scientists placed in AI governance organisations and national AI safety institutes, producing joint designs for compute and model-verification regimes. Risks: technical work on compute verification already exists inside AI governance, so the fellowship should bring regime-design and inspection know-how rather than duplicate hardware research. Former inspectors may also be bound by confidentiality.
steps: Approach CNTR before December 2026 about bridge funding that keeps its verification group alive while a fellowship is designed.

Recruit a first cohort through VERTIC, CTBTO and OPCW alumni networks and the PRIF and IFSH arms-control networks, and place fellows with oxford-martin-ai-governance-initiative, institute-for-security-and-technology or national AI safety institutes.

Ask each fellow for a short design paper on one verifiable AI commitment (for example a compute threshold or a model-evaluation obligation), tested in a tabletop exercise with stanford-center-for-international-security-and-c or un-institute-for-disarmament-research.
openings.evidence: No verification body (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) is on the map, and gap (b) in the discovery notes says this expertise has barely reached compute governance. prif-emerging-disruptive-technologies-research-g's funding ends in December 2026. institute-for-security-and-technology's accelerator (26 fellows) is the model to copy. A quick search found academic papers on lessons from nuclear verification for AI treaties and a CTBTO fellowship limited to nuclear work, but no AI verification placement scheme.

openings.title: Model safety clauses for collective agreements at labs and data suppliers
openings.summary: The map has 17 labour organisations: 16 are framed around present harms, and the only bridge is the UTAW/Unite campaign at Google DeepMind. No AI-safety organisation works with unions. A small unit that drafts and tests safety clauses would give the field a lever with legal force: safety representatives, a right to refuse unsafe deployment, whistleblower protection, and fair-work standards for the people who do RLHF and red-teaming.
openings.detail: UTAW members asked Google for recognition in May 2026. Google refused but agreed to ACAS talks limited to pay, holidays and hours, so what can be bargained over is now the live question. The material for a clause bank already exists: the TUC's model AI bill (drafted by Robin Allen KC and Dee Masters), UK health-and-safety representative law, institute-for-the-future-of-work's impact assessments, Fairwork's AI principles and supplier audits (Sama, Appen), and the data-worker code of conduct from aapti-institute and Karya. On the supply side, alphabet-workers-union-cwa has organised Google's AI raters, and data-labelers-association (878+ members, Nairobi) and data-workers-inquiry speak for the people who produce safety-relevant labels. Success would be a clause bank used in at least one recognition agreement, and a safety funder or lab committing to Fairwork standards for its red-teaming and RLHF suppliers. The risks: labs will resist, the work may be seen as partisan, unions may put job losses ahead of safety, and lab funding could co-opt worker voice.
steps: Fund the TUC model-bill drafters or institute-for-the-future-of-work to draft a short clause bank on safety representatives, the right to refuse, and whistleblower protection, adapted from UK health-and-safety law.
Offer it to UTAW/Unite and AWU-CWA for their campaigns, with the-ai-whistleblower-initiative advising on protections.
Ask safety funders and labs to adopt Fairwork's AI principles for their RLHF and red-teaming suppliers, with data-labelers-association and data-workers-inquiry consulted on the terms.
int/a's London hub convenes UTAW, the TUC, IFOW and AIWI; all four are in London.
openings.evidence: econ_labour: 17 entries, 16 adjacent, 1 bridge, 0 core, and all 17 framed as present harms or structural. The membership-bodies notes found no union framing AI as a civilisation-scale loss of bargaining power, and no AI-safety organisation working with unions. 8 economics entries tag 'people'.

openings.title: Human-rights due diligence for frontier AI, tested through investors
openings.summary: In September 2026 the UN human rights chief asked frontier AI companies for human-rights due diligence that includes agreed safety standards, incident reporting and independent monitoring. Nobody has yet written what that means for catastrophic risks. A joint team from business-and-human-rights and frontier-safety evaluation would write that protocol and pilot it, using investors and national human rights institutions to press for adoption.
openings.detail: The UN Guiding Principles already rank harms by scale, scope and irremediability, a test that fits catastrophic, irreversible risks better than most AI-ethics frameworks. They come with tools already in use: OHCHR B-Tech's foundation-model papers and its product workstream with BSR (adjacent), DIHR's guide to fundamental rights impact assessments and its NHRI Digital Rights Alliance (adjacent), the Council of Europe's HUDERIA method (adjacent), OECD National Contact Points, and engagement by faith-based investors through ICCR and the Investor Alliance for Human Rights (religion>law, adjacent). Frontier safety frameworks set capability thresholds and evaluations, but they offer no rights-based remedy and no external route for complaints. None of the 93 law entries connects the two sides. Success would be a published protocol that maps the elements of frontier safety frameworks onto the Guiding Principles' steps. It would be used in at least one investor engagement and one NHRI review, and cited by AISIs. There are three risks. Due diligence can turn into box-ticking. Rights groups such as Derechos Digitales and Fundación Vía Libre are sceptical of x-risk framing. And labs may welcome a soft standard as a way to avoid regulation, so the protocol has to keep the Guiding Principles' remedy and independent-monitoring elements.
steps: Bring B-Tech, DIHR and a frontier evaluator (an AISI or an independent evaluation group) together for a short drafting sprint on how the Guiding Principles' test of severity maps onto capability thresholds and incident reporting.
Pilot it with ICCR members and other responsible investors that hold shares in frontier-lab parent companies, as engagement asks for the 2027 AGM season.
Ask one national human rights institution, DIHR, to review a lab's published safety framework against the protocol.
Feed the results into the Council of Europe Convention's Conference of the Parties and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
openings.evidence: Türk's letter of September 2026 asks frontier AI companies for exactly this. B-Tech, DIHR, the Council of Europe and ICCR are all adjacent, and all transfer into institutions. Of 93 law profiles, 52 are framed around present harms and 2 around catastrophic risk. The sociotech angle notes list this as a bridge no organisation owns.

openings.title: A desk turning chatbot-harm court records into evidence on lab safety
openings.summary: Chatbot-harm lawsuits produce filings, expert reports and testimony about how labs tested and shipped their models. Nobody reads these as safety evidence, and settlements can bury them. A small legal-research desk would collect, code and publish what the public record shows, and push for settlements and remedies that disclose more.
openings.detail: The Tech Justice Law Project (bridge) was counsel in Garcia v. Character Technologies, and in 2026 it filed Carrier and Lines v. OpenAI Foundation. In January 2026 Character.AI and Google agreed to settle five teen-harm suits, Garcia among them, which shows how quickly evidence can vanish into settlements. Trackers exist, such as TJLP's TRAL tracker with Knight-Georgetown and Georgetown CCT, but they count cases. They do not extract what the cases reveal about evaluations, red-teaming, known risks and decisions to ship. Others need that factual base: the ALI's Principles of the Law on civil liability for AI (adjacent), OII's 'careless speech' work, and safety researchers writing about lab practice. Success would be a public, coded record of the safety-relevant facts in every major AI-harm case, cited by AISIs, the ALI reporters and model-spec authors. It would also mean settlement terms that require disclosure and independent monitoring. The risks are real. Protective orders and sealed discovery limit what is public. The desk could look like plaintiff advocacy, so it needs a neutral host such as a law-school clinic, with input from defence lawyers. And most cases concern companion harms rather than catastrophic risk, although what they show about how labs decide to ship carries over.
steps: List the AI-harm dockets (the OpenAI and Character.AI suicide and psychosis suits, Social Media Victims Law Center cases, the FTC's 2025 orders to companion-chatbot makers) and code public filings against a template drawn from frontier safety frameworks.
Host the desk in a US law-school clinic, with advisers from TJLP and the defence bar and one safety researcher to frame the coding.
Where protective orders cover safety-relevant material, file public-interest motions to unseal, and draft model settlement terms with disclosure and independent-monitor clauses.
Publish a brief twice a year for AISIs, the ALI reporters and lab safety teams.
openings.evidence: Law x assurance has 34 entries, but only 4 of 93 law entries transfer into the model. TJLP is the only litigation organisation on the map. The sociotech angle notes list this as an unowned bridge ('litigation-to-safety translation desk'). Garcia was settled in January 2026.

openings.title: An African philosophy research line inside Africa's AI-safety organisations
openings.summary: Africa's AI-safety organisations work in law, policy and technical fields, and none draws on philosophy. The one African philosophy entry on the map has been inactive since 2022. A funded philosophy line, hosted by an existing safety body, would bring Ubuntu and other African relational ethics into alignment targets and debates on moral status.
openings.detail: Ubuntu-based AI ethics is now a substantial academic literature: Sabelo Mhlambi's work, a 2026 dissertation on Ubuntu as a paradigm for AI governance, and proposals to build it into African health-AI research ethics. Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem of the University of Pretoria chaired the expert group that drafted UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation, and she co-authored a 2026 Delphi study ranking AI risks. Yet the angle notes found Ubuntu scholars and no organisation, and her CAIR group (ethics-of-ai-research-group-centre-for-ai-resear) shows no activity after 2022. Meanwhile Africa's safety bodies are growing: ilina-program (core, on the classic map), african-hub-on-ai-safety-peace-and-security (launched by UCT and global-center-on-ai-governance), cape-institute-for-safe-ai-formerly-ai-safety-so and equiano-institute. Success would be a 2-3 year research line with a few fellows, hosted by one of these bodies. It would publish on, for example, what relational personhood implies for AI moral status (a direct input to eleos-ai-research and nyu-center-for-mind-ethics-and-policy) and what communal consent implies for public input to model specs, and it would feed the multi-tradition spec review above. The risks are presenting Ubuntu as one doctrine, thin senior capacity, and drifting back into general AI ethics without a safety question.
steps: Approach african-hub-on-ai-safety-peace-and-security and global-center-on-ai-governance about hosting one or two philosophy fellows.
Ask Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem whether the Pretoria CAIR ethics group could be revived around AI risk and moral status.
Fund 3-5 African philosophy fellowships attached to ilina-program's existing fellowship.
Commission one paper on Ubuntu personhood and AI moral status, and put it into the digital-minds field's venues.
openings.evidence: Philosophy by region: africa 1 (ethics-of-ai-research-group-centre-for-ai-resear, unverified, last activity 2022), latin_america 0, mena 0. Of the 11 African organisations on the whole map, none lists philosophy as a tradition. Angle notes (faith/knowledge traditions, gap d): 'Ubuntu has scholars ... but no organisation'. A web search (Oct 2026) found academic Ubuntu-AI work but no standing centre.

arts.overview: Arts, narrative and futures brings imagination as a working method: the scenarios, wargames and stories through which publics and decision-makers picture AI, and the futures and technology-assessment bodies that turn foresight into policy. The map holds 46 organisations here (9 core, 11 bridge, 20 adjacent, 7 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map). The core is scenario and narrative work inside the safety community, such as the AI Futures Project, Intelligence Rising, Existential Hope, Tarbell and Geodesic Research. The outer rings hold futures institutes (Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies, Institute for the Future, Sitra, Europe's parliamentary technology-assessment offices), arts institutions (Serpentine Arts Technologies, AIxDESIGN, Better Images of AI) and the translators' and linguists' professional bodies.
arts.missing: Narrative craft has barely met the finding that stories in training data shape model behaviour, and the futures profession itself (the World Futures Studies Federation, UNESCO Futures Literacy, the School of International Futures) has no sustained AI-risk programme, so the field's scenarios come almost entirely from forecasters inside it.

essays.funders:
Money for this wider field comes from three groups that rarely fund together. The AI-safety funders (the Survival and Flourishing Fund, Coefficient Giving, the Future of Life Institute, Macroscopic Ventures, Longview and the Navigation Fund) fund almost entirely in the core and bridge rings, and mostly in the formal and life sciences, consciousness and AI welfare, and forecasting. Public research money for AI safety, such as ARIA's £59 million Safeguarded AI programme and the £27 million Alignment Project led by the UK AI Security Institute, follows similar lines with a stronger pull towards mathematics and verification.

The second group funds the adjacent ring and frames AI as present harm or public interest. Humanity AI has committed $500 million over five years from ten foundations, Current AI reports $404 million pledged for public-interest AI, Omidyar Network, Mozilla and the European AI & Society Fund back rights and accountability groups, and Anthropic's Economic Futures programme has a $200 million research fund. These funders reach the law, economics and democracy traditions that hold most of the map's organisations, but rarely the questions about the AI itself.

The third group funds the traditions this map is about without any AI-safety framing. Templeton World Charity Foundation put about $2.8 million into three Diverse Intelligences hubs in 2025, and the John Templeton Foundation's Future of Intelligence venture will give more than $60 million over 2026 to 2028. Lilly Endowment gave $50.8 million to Notre Dame's DELTA network for faith-based formation in an age of AI. Lloyd's Register Foundation (a £300 million grant portfolio, with £13.9 million to York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy) and UL Research Institutes fund engineering safety, and Carnegie Corporation funds the AI-and-nuclear work of the peace tradition.

Some traditions have no dedicated funder for AI work at all. The contemplative world's grant-makers (Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera, Templeton Religion Trust) were found to make no AI grants, which helps explain why 22 of the 40 contemplative organisations sit in the potential ring. No AI-safety funder backs any of the Indigenous-led organisations, and the psychological support services for the field's own workers run on very little.

The most promising moves for funders are co-funding pairs that cross these groups: a safety funder with Templeton on comparative cognition and consciousness science; with Lloyd's Register Foundation or UL Research Institutes on placing system-safety engineers; with Carnegie Corporation on verification expertise; with Mind & Life and the contemplative funders on a contemplative-science call; and with faith funders on carrying frontier-risk concerns into religious norm-setting. The newest and largest funder of all, the OpenAI Foundation, holds a stake in OpenAI worth more than $100 billion, and where it chooses to sit among these groups will matter more than any single grant.
essays.bridges:
Several problems on the map are worked on by two or more communities that barely know each other. Power concentration is the clearest. Inside the safety field, Formation Research, Longview's power-concentration call, the Alignment of Complex Systems group's work on gradual disempowerment and the Post-AGI workshops treat it as a structural risk from advanced AI. Outside it, the Open Markets Institute, the AI Now Institute, MIT's Stone Center, the unions (the TUC, UTAW and Unite at Google DeepMind, the Alphabet Workers Union) and the financial-stability supervisors work on the same concentration with antitrust law, collective bargaining and macroprudential tools. The two sides cite different literatures and meet at different conferences.

The same split runs through human minds. The UK AI Security Institute's societal-resilience team and the AI-welfare groups study persuasion, sycophancy and attribution of mind from the model's side; psychiatrists at King's College London, Aarhus and Beth Israel Deaconess, the psychoanalysts' AI commission, BACP and the child-development groups (Common Sense Media, Fairplay, 5Rights) study the same harms from the person's side. Among consciousness researchers, 27 of 28 work on AI moral status, while 47 of 65 psychology organisations work on protecting minds and none works on moral status, although both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious.

Law repeats the pattern: the x-risk legal groups on the classic map have little contact with the 91 rights, liability and accountability organisations, of which only 2 frame the stakes as catastrophic. Democracy splits between its forecasting strand, which the safety field has adopted (6 of the tradition's 9 classic-map entries are forecasting or epistemics groups), and its legitimacy strand of assemblies and deliberation, which it has not. Peace splits between arms control and Track II diplomacy, which work on AI, and peacebuilding and mediation, which mostly do not.

Connecting these worlds would yield more than goodwill. Each side holds something the other lacks: evaluation methods and threat models on one side, clinical evidence, legal remedies, institutional legitimacy and decades of practice on the other. Several openings below are bridges of exactly this kind: shared evaluations built with clinicians, translation fellowships, joint research agendas and convenings with a fixed output.
essays.inta:
The map says something specific about int/a's own milieu. Contemplative and integral organisations number 40, and 22 of them are potential partners with little or no AI work; only 2 sit in the core. The int/a principle badges were given sparingly, and only 2 organisations carry the "inner work, outer change" badge: integral altruism itself and Connecting Intelligence. The traditions int/a draws on hold a great deal of relevant knowledge and very few bridges to where AI is being built and governed.

That points to a role suited to a volunteer community with hubs in London (66 organisations on the map are active there), Paris (28) and Berlin (25). int/a can translate: write the briefs that restate AI-safety problems in the language of contemplative science, faith traditions or bioethics, and carry them to the people who can act. It can convene where pace and trust matter, such as dialogues between AI-safety and AI-ethics researchers, or workshops joining clinicians and consciousness researchers, in the spirit of moving at the speed of wisdom. And it can model care for the people doing the work, with the safeguards that the MAPLE allegations show are needed.

The suggestion in the brief that the mapping itself could be the int/a project is the strongest of all. This map was made quickly by AI agents; a version corrected tradition by tradition by practitioners would be more accurate, and the process would build the relationships the openings depend on. A post per tradition for the int/a Substack or the EA Forum, and a one-page brief for funders, would make the work legible to new funders, which was the original aim.

Two cautions. The integral and contemplative world has its own failure modes, from guru dynamics to grand theory without evidence, and int/a's credibility with funders depends on holding its own proposals to the same tests it asks of others: the contemplative self-preservation study and the wisdom benchmark below are designed to produce publishable null results as readily as positive ones. And the map should not become a way of claiming the field's adjacent traditions for int/a: most of these organisations have never heard of it, and the first step is listening to them.
essays.people:
The people who build, govern, fund and research AI are the least served part of this map. Only 10 organisations offer direct care or support to individuals, and they are fragile: AI Safety Support has been paused since July 2023, Upgradable has done little since early 2025, Mental Health Navigator runs on about £1,200 a year, and Rethink Wellbeing is not specific to AI. The AI Whistleblower Initiative supports insiders who raise concerns, and the Data Labelers Association and the Data Workers' Inquiry speak for the workforce that produces safety-relevant labels.

The need is documented. The seed list cites a 2026 write-up of survey data reporting burnout among 59% of AI-safety respondents, and forum posts describe stress that cannot be taken to an outside therapist because of non-disclosure agreements, anticipatory grief about the future, and isolation outside the main hubs. Psychology on this map studies users, children and patients far more than it studies the people and institutions steering AI: no organisation measures safety culture inside labs or studies how decision-makers perceive the race.

Other fields already know how to do much of this. Humanitarian organisations have staff-care guidelines for people exposed to distressing material; governments have clinicians cleared to hear classified material; climate psychology runs groups for distress about the future; chaplaincy has codified ethics of presence and referral; medicine and engineering have professional oaths and just-culture reporting. None of these has been adapted for AI.

Any support offered to AI people needs safeguards from the start. The most visible contemplative programme for technologists, MAPLE, faces serious, detailed public allegations of high-control dynamics, contested by its supporters. Independent governance, clear complaint routes, no discouraging of outside therapy, and norms on sleep, money and hierarchy are the minimum, and the openings below build them in.

summary_points: The map holds 722 organisations across 14 traditions. Only 64 (9%) appear on the aisafety.com field map, so most of this landscape is invisible from the field's standard directory.

Visibility falls with distance from the sciences: 15% of Sciences & engineering entries are on the classic map, against 3% of Minds & inner life. Consciousness and AI minds has 11 core organisations and none on the classic map.

The biggest bodies of knowledge sit furthest from the safety frame. Law, rights & society has 91 organisations, 2 of them core and 2 framing the stakes as catastrophic. Religion has 50 and 1 core entry; Indigenous & decolonial knowledges has none.

Adjacent fields mostly talk to their own people: 123 of 722 organisations move their knowledge into AI models and 26 into the people who build and govern AI, while 77 of the 183 in Minds & inner life mainly convene their own community.

AI safety has imported the artefacts of older safety cultures (safety cases, incident databases, risk thresholds) but not their institutions: no confidential near-miss reporting, no independent accident investigation, no measurement of safety culture and no bioethics-style monitoring board was found.
The inner side of the field is the thinnest part of the map: 10 organisations offer direct care, one of them paused since 2023, and only 2 carry int/a's "inner work, outer change" badge.
Coverage leans Anglophone: 55% of entries are in North America or the UK and Ireland, and 54 are Indigenous-led or centred on the Majority World. Some of what looks empty is a limit of the search.
42 openings for founders, funders and int/a follow, ranked. The first ten are flagged as places to start.

findings.title: Most of the wider field is invisible from the standard map
findings.body: Of 722 organisations, 64 are on the aisafety.com field map. None of the 28 consciousness and AI-minds organisations is there although 11 are core, and neither is any of the 40 contemplative or 15 Indigenous & decolonial entries. The classic map is a good guide to the core; it is not a guide to the knowledge around it.

findings.title: AI safety has absorbed formal science and little else
findings.body: The formal and physical sciences are the one tradition the field already owns: 17 of 32 organisations are core, 12 are on the classic map and only 1 is adjacent. Much of the new money of 2025 and 2026 has gone to mathematics, learning theory and verification, for example Coefficient Giving's $10 million to the new Mathematical AI Safety Institute and ARIA's £59 million Safeguarded AI programme.

findings.title: The largest knowledge bases are furthest out
findings.body: The adjacent ring is the largest, with 320 organisations. Law (91), democracy and collective intelligence (68), psychology (65) and economics (60) are the biggest traditions, and all of them sit mostly outside the safety frame. Their methods (litigation, assemblies, clinical evidence, antitrust and supervision) are tested at scale but rarely applied to frontier AI.

findings.title: Knowledge rarely reaches the builders
findings.body: Only 26 organisations change the people who build, govern and fund AI, against 123 that work on the models and many more that inform institutions or convene their own community. Psychology studies users and children; nobody on the map studies the psychology of the labs and governments steering AI.

findings.title: Artefacts without institutions
findings.body: The safety and risk sciences have 67 organisations on the map, 3 of them on the classic map. Frontier AI has taken their safety cases, risk thresholds and incident databases, but not confidential near-miss reporting, independent investigation, just culture or peer review. Philosophy shows the same split: AI safety adopted its theories of value, while 17 of the 18 applied-ethics and bioethics bodies, which hold fifty years of oversight practice, sit in the adjacent ring.

findings.title: Two communities study the same people from opposite sides
findings.body: 27 of the 28 consciousness organisations work on AI moral status; 47 of the 65 psychology organisations work on protecting human minds, and none on moral status. Both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious, the welfare researchers to take the belief seriously and the clinicians to treat its harms, and they do not work together.

findings.title: int/a's own milieu is mostly potential
findings.body: 22 of the 40 contemplative and integral organisations (55%) are potential partners, the highest share of any tradition, and only 2 are core. The contemplative world's funders make no AI grants, and the groups turning contemplative insight into alignment proposals have not yet tested them against the safety field's own evaluations.

findings.title: Religion has reach, and a shallow bridge
findings.body: The 50 religious organisations include norm-setters that speak for billions and have already issued AI rulings (the Holy See's Magnifica Humanitas, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy's Resolution 258, ICESCO's Riyadh Charter), but none of those rulings addresses loss of control. The main bridge to AI safety is a single round of FLI grants to faith communities (16 grants, about $1.36 million).

findings.title: Democracy's forecasting strand made it in; its legitimacy strand didn't
findings.body: 6 of the 9 democracy and collective-intelligence organisations on the classic map are forecasting or epistemics groups. Assemblies, deliberative polling and consensus conferences, the tradition's machinery of legitimacy, have not reached the decisions the safety field cares most about, such as capability thresholds, pauses or AI moral status.

findings.title: Multi-agent risk is thinly staffed across traditions
findings.body: Only 36 organisations work on populations of interacting AI agents. Economics has 2 of 60; peace has none, though conflict between parties is its core subject; collective-behaviour biologists and evolutionary game theorists sit in the potential ring. The disciplines that study cooperation and conflict among many agents are mostly not yet looking at AI agents.

openings_intro: Eighteen analysts, one for each tradition and four for cross-cutting questions, read the profiles and statistics and proposed 52 openings. Five of the eighteen and the final synthesiser did not complete their work, so the selection, merging and ranking below, the arts note and the cross-cutting essays were done in the main session. Each opening names the part of the map it would fill and who is nearby. They were not individually tested against the open web; ten of the strongest were spot-checked for prior work, and one was narrowed as a result. Treat each as a well-grounded hypothesis to check before acting.
